message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"20.11","text":"Just as a meal was about to be served to us, someone slipped in and said, “Appion the Many-Victor has just arrived from Antioch with Annoubion and is staying as Simon’s guest.” When our father heard this, he rejoiced and said to Peter, “If you permit me, I will go greet Appion and Annoubion, who have been my friends from earliest youth. Perhaps I may persuade Annoubion to debate Clement about nativity.” Peter said, “I permit it, and I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship. But consider how, by God’s providence, everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony. I say this because Annoubion’s arrival has proved advantageous to you.” Our father replied, “I truly see that this is so.” After saying this, he went to Simon.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ἀππίων ὁ πλειστονίκης","chosen":"Appion the Many-Victor","rationale":"πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet denoting numerous victories rather than silently transliterated as another personal name."},{"source_quote":"περὶ γενέσεως","chosen":"about nativity","rationale":"In this debate setting γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, particularly as a subject of astrological determinism; “birth” or “genesis” remains possible more generally."},{"source_quote":"ἐπαινῶ τὰ φίλων σε πληροῦντα μέρη","chosen":"I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship","rationale":"The idiom describes performing the part or duties belonging to friends; the English avoids reproducing the awkward literal image of “parts.”"},{"source_quote":"πανταχόθεν συντρέχει τὰ πρὸς τὴν σὴν πληροφορίαν οἰκείαν ἀποτελοῦντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν","chosen":"everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony","rationale":"οἰκείαν is taken with τὴν ἁρμονίαν as “fitting”; attachment to πληροφορίαν, yielding something like “your own assurance,” is also grammatically possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"20.12","text":"As for us who were with Peter, we spent the whole night asking questions one after another, remaining awake because of the pleasure and joy produced by what was being said. When the night was already beginning somehow to brighten, Peter looked at me and my brothers and said, “I am perplexed about what your father decided.” While he was saying this, our father arrived there and found Peter discussing him with us. Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained why he had slept outside. We stared at him in astonishment, seeing Simon’s appearance but hearing the voice of our father Faustus. As we recoiled from him and regarded him with loathing, our father was astounded at being treated so harshly and hostilely by us. Only Peter, who saw his natural form, said to us, “Why do you push your father away in disgust?” We and our mother replied, “To us this man looks like Simon, though he has our father’s voice.” Peter said, “For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes his appearance too is visible as it really is: he is not Simon but Faustus, your father.” Then, looking directly at our father too, he said, “......... appearance of yours is not visible to them, but Simon’s—the most impious man’s—is; and to us .........”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"νήφοντες ἐνυκτερεύσαμεν","chosen":"we spent the whole night ... remaining awake","rationale":"Here νήφω concerns wakeful alertness during the night rather than literal abstinence from intoxication; “remaining clear-minded” is possible but less closely fitted to the overnight setting."},{"source_quote":"καὶ ἀθυμοῦντα ἰδὼν προσαγορεύσας ἀπελογήσατο","chosen":"Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained","rationale":"The unexpressed person seen as disheartened is taken to be Peter, whom the arriving father has just found discussing him. Reference to another participant is formally possible but less natural in context."},{"source_quote":"μόνος δὲ Πέτρος τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτοῦ ὁρῶν μορφὴν","chosen":"Only Peter, who saw his natural form","rationale":"κατὰ φύσιν identifies the form belonging to Faustus’s real nature, in contrast to the magically imposed appearance."},{"source_quote":"Ὑμῖν μὲν ἡ ἀμάγευτος αὐτοῦ φωνὴ μόνη γνώριμός ἐστιν, ἐμοῦ δὲ τοῖς ἀμαγεύτοις ὀφθαλμοῖς","chosen":"For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes","rationale":"ἀμάγευτος is rendered as freedom from magical alteration or deception, preserving the repetition applied first to the voice and then to Peter’s eyes."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"......... όν σου εἶδος αὐτοῖς οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνος τοῦ ἀσεβεστάτου καὶ ἡμῖν .........","issue":"The selected edition prints two lacunae of nine dots each. After the first gap, only όν survives, either as an isolated form or as the ending of a lost word, and it cannot receive a secure independent English rendering. Both nine-dot gaps remain explicit, and no restoration of either gap or of the broken construction is supplied.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"20.13","text":"While Peter was saying this, one of the advance messengers came in from Antioch ..........., saying to Peter, “I want you to know, my lord, that Simon, by publicly performing many marvels in Antioch and calling you a magician and a sorcerer, has stirred them to such hatred that every person among those staying there longs to taste your very flesh. Consequently, when we advance messengers and our brothers whom you had planted with Simon saw the city gnashing furiously against you, we met secretly in one place to consider what must be done. While we were at a loss, Cornelius arrived, a centurion sent by Caesar to the governor of the province—the man whom the Lord had healed at Caesarea when he was demon-possessed. We summoned him secretly, explained the reason for our discouragement, and appealed to him for help. He very eagerly promised to frighten Simon into flight, provided, of course, that we assisted him in his undertaking. When we readily promised to do everything, he said, ‘While I keep watch and secretly claim through many friends that I have come to arrest him and am searching for him—because Caesar has executed many magicians, learned the facts about him, and sent me to seek him so that he might punish him just like the magicians before him—let your people who are with him also report, as though they had secretly heard it somewhere, that I have been sent to arrest him. Perhaps when he hears it, he will take fright and flee.’ Now although we had considered doing something else, this is nevertheless what happened. For after he had heard it from many outsiders—who secretly told him while currying his favor in important matters—and also from our planted agents inside, and had received what he took to be advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw. He therefore escaped from Antioch and, as we have heard, came here with Athenodorus. We consequently advise you not yet to enter that city, until we know whether, in his absence, they will be able to hypolēsai with respect to his slander against you.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τις τῶν προόδων","chosen":"one of the advance messengers","rationale":"πρόοδοι denotes people who go ahead or operate in advance; “forerunners” is possible but less clear in this organizational context."},{"source_quote":"πολλὰ τεράστια ποιῶν","chosen":"performing many marvels","rationale":"τεράστια denotes extraordinary, portent-like feats; “wonders” or, with a hostile nuance, “monstrous feats” are alternatives."},{"source_quote":"μάγον σε ὀνομάζων καὶ γόητα","chosen":"calling you a magician and a sorcerer","rationale":"The two accusations are kept distinct. γόης can also mean “conjurer,” “charlatan,” or “impostor,” but the magical context supports “sorcerer.”"},{"source_quote":"σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου","chosen":"to taste your very flesh","rationale":"αὐτῶν is taken intensively with σαρκῶν, heightening the violent image; a strictly reflexive reference to the flesh of some other group is less natural here."},{"source_quote":"ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος","chosen":"the man whom the Lord had healed at Caesarea when he was demon-possessed","rationale":"The main rendering takes ὅν as referring to Cornelius. Because the provincial governor is the nearer masculine antecedent, reference to the governor is grammatically possible and remains an alternative."},{"source_quote":"Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περισκοποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος","chosen":"While I keep watch and secretly claim through many friends that I have come to arrest him and am searching for him","rationale":"The genitive construction presents Cornelius as maintaining surveillance while causing or allowing the claim to circulate through friends. The precise attachment of διὰ πολλῶν φίλων and κρύφα is flexible."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἔξω εἰς τὰ μεγάλα αὐτῷ χαριζομένων","chosen":"outsiders ... currying his favor in important matters","rationale":"The phrase is understood as describing outsiders who seek Simon’s favor in substantial affairs; “who did him great favors” is another viable rendering."},{"source_quote":"ὡς παρ’ ἰδίων γνώμην εἰληφὼς ὑποστέλλεσθαι ἔγνω","chosen":"having received what he took to be advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw","rationale":"In this receive-from construction, γνώμη is taken as “advice” or “counsel,” distinguishing it from merely hearing the report. The broader senses “judgment” or “information” remain possible."},{"source_quote":"τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται","chosen":"in his absence, they will be able to hypolēsai with respect to his slander against you","rationale":"Because no secure lexical and morphological account of the printed ὑπολῆσαι has been established, the verb is transliterated rather than assigned the unsupported meaning “recover from.” The genitive phrase is represented neutrally with “with respect to.” A conjectural ὑπολῆξαι could mean “cease” or “abate,” but that is not the selected edition’s reading."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας ........... λέγων Πέτρῳ","issue":"The selected edition prints an eleven-dot lacuna between “from Antioch” and “saying to Peter.” The missing wording is unavailable; all eleven dots are retained, and no identity, description, or adverb is restored.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται","issue":"The image-checked selected edition prints ὑπολῆσαι. No secure lexical or morphological analysis of this form in the construction with the genitive τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς has been established, so its meaning remains unresolved. The context may suggest cessation or abatement, and ὑπολῆξαι would be the regular aorist infinitive of ὑπολήγω, but that reading is conjectural. The translation therefore leaves the verb transliterated rather than supplying an unsupported sense. This unresolved source or meaning problem blocks publication.","proposed_reading":"ὑπολῆξαι","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"20.14","text":"When the advance messenger had reported these things, Peter looked directly at our father and said, “Do you hear, Faustus? Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician, as is now evident. Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm, he fled in fear, placing his own form upon you so that, when you died, grief would come upon your children.” Hearing this, our father wept and lamented, saying, “You have judged correctly, Peter. Annoubion ...... of mine, because he loved me, cryptically disclosed the plot, and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ Σίμωνος τοῦ μάγου ἡ μεταμόρφωσίς σου γέγονεν","chosen":"Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician","rationale":"The construction presents Simon as the agent responsible for Faustus’s altered appearance."},{"source_quote":"Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν","chosen":"Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm","rationale":"ἐπὶ κακῷ indicates harmful or punitive intent without specifying the precise punishment. The contextual interpretation of Caesar as the seeker is retained despite the printed case irregularity disclosed in source_issues."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σοὶ περιθεὶς μορφήν","chosen":"placing his own form upon you","rationale":"The concrete image of putting Simon’s appearance around or upon Faustus is retained rather than reduced to simple resemblance."},{"source_quote":"μυστηριωδῶς τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ἐξέφηγε","chosen":"cryptically disclosed the plot","rationale":"μυστηριωδῶς indicates an indirect, mysterious, or cryptic disclosure; ἐπιβουλή is a hostile plot or design."},{"source_quote":"καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος","chosen":"and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer","rationale":"The first-person speaker and the following first-person ἤμην support “I,” but the precise ending of ἐπίστευ- and any further lost wording remain unavailable. The English does not supply an object of belief."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν","issue":"The edition prints the genitive Καίσαρος, although the contextual reading takes Caesar as the subject of ζητεῖν, for which the accusative Καίσαρα would ordinarily be expected in this infinitival construction after νομίσας. Καίσαρα is only a proposed grammatical regularization; the translation retains the contextually defensible interpretation without claiming that the regularization is printed.","proposed_reading":"Καίσαρα","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"Ἀννουβίων ...... μού με φιλῶν","issue":"The selected edition prints a six-dot lacuna before μού. The surviving “of mine” indicates a lost description or relationship, but its wording cannot be recovered. All six dots remain explicit, and no description is restored.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος","issue":"The selected edition prints ten dots immediately after the surviving verbal stem ἐπίστευ-. The precise verbal ending and any following words are unavailable; the ten-dot gap is retained without supplying an object or other lost content.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"20.15","text":"After our father said this, not long afterward ....... to us, reporting Simon’s flight to us and that he had set out for Judea that very night. He found our father beating himself and saying with lamentation, “Alas, wretch that I am! Though I heard that he was a magician, miserable man that I am, I refused to believe it. After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day, I quickly returned to my former calamity of being unknown.” Our mother, lamenting, kept tearing out her hair, while we groaned in distress over our father’s alteration, unable to understand what on earth it was. When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed. Before everyone, Peter said to us children, “Believe me: this is Faustus, your father. I therefore command you to pay him the regard due to a father, for God will provide some occasion through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again.” After saying this to us, he looked at our father and said, “I permitted you to greet Appion and Annoubion because you acknowledge that they have been your friends since childhood, not to associate with Simon the magician.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εὗρε δὲ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν κοπτόμενον","chosen":"He found our father beating himself","rationale":"κόπτομαι can describe striking oneself as an embodied act of mourning; the accompanying lament supports retaining that concrete action."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγνωσθεὶς συμβίῳ καὶ τέκνοις","chosen":"After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day","rationale":"ἐπιγινώσκω here concerns recognition of identity, while σύμβιος denotes one’s spouse or life-partner; the context identifies Faustus’s wife."},{"source_quote":"τὴν προτέραν τῆς ἀγνοίας ἦλθον συμφοράν","chosen":"I returned to my former calamity of being unknown","rationale":"ἀγνοία is understood contextually as his family’s failure to recognize him, not merely as intellectual ignorance."},{"source_quote":"Ἀννουβίων δὲ ταῦτα ἀκούων καὶ ὁρῶν ἀχανὴς ἔστη","chosen":"When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed","rationale":"ἀχανής preserves the visible image of standing open-mouthed in stunned astonishment; “stood aghast” or “stood dumbfounded” conveys the reaction but not the image as directly."},{"source_quote":"ὡς πατρὶ προσέχειν","chosen":"to pay him the regard due to a father","rationale":"προσέχειν calls for attention, adherence, or care toward Faustus in his paternal identity; “attend to him as a father” is more literal but less idiomatic."},{"source_quote":"δι᾽ ἧς τὴν Σίμωνος ἀποδυσάμενος μορφὴν τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν προδήλως ἀναδείξει πάλιν","chosen":"through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again","rationale":"The main rendering takes Faustus as the understood subject of “stripping off” and “revealing,” since the middle image naturally depicts him shedding Simon’s form. The nearest explicit subject is God, so taking God as the agent of the removal and revelation is grammatically possible, though less natural with the stripping image."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ ....... πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν Σίμωνος ἡμῖν δηλῶν φυγὴν","issue":"The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna after “not long afterward.” The missing subject and finite expression governing “to us” are unavailable. All seven dots remain explicit, and the arriving reporter is not identified.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
